sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Driving world models usually generate videos from six pinhole cameras with separate optical centres and small overlaps, and must learn to keep these views consistent. We present PanDWM, which stitches them into one $360^\circ$ panoramic band. Camera boundaries then fall inside one image, so keeping the views consistent means keeping the image continuous, and each pixel still records its camera ray. Conditioned on layouts, a causal student generates the band window by window in four steps; it is distilled from a causal teacher and trained on its own rollouts. A feed-forward decoder lifts each frame along these rays into 3D Gaussians, and static Gaussians from neighbouring frames complete them into 4D scenes. On nuScenes, scored in one stitched $360^\circ$ view, PanDWM has lower FID and FVD than the multi-camera baselines at $8$-$46\times$ their speed, and keeps its 50-step teacher's FID while lowering FVD by 22-25%.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: 1. Introduction Driving world models usually generate videos from six pinhole cameras with separate optical centres and small overlaps, and must learn to keep these views consistent. We present PanDWM, which stitches them into one 360 panoramic band. Camera boundaries then fall inside one image, so keeping the views consistent means keeping the image continuous, and each pixel still records its camera ray. Conditioned on layouts, causal student generates the band window by window in four steps; it is distilled from causal teacher and trained on its own rollouts. feed-forward decoder lifts each frame along these rays into 3D Gaussians, and static Gaussians from neighbouring frames complete them into 4D scenes. On nuScenes, scored in one stitched 360 view, PanDWM has lower FID and FVD than the multi-camera baselines at 8 46 their speed, and keeps its 50-step teachers FID while lowering FVD by 2225%. Code: https://github. com/AIGeeksGroup/PanDWM . Website: https:// aigeeksgroup.github.io/PanDWM . Driving world models predict future surround-view video from scene layouts and past frames, and serve as controllable simulators for autonomous driving. Their predictions must stay consistent across cameras and over long rollouts. Simulating trajectories that leave the recorded one also requires rendering the predicted scene from new viewpoints. Existing layout-conditioned generators [5, 15, 53, 76] represent the surround view as six perspective videos, one per camera. This representation cuts the scene at every camera boundary. The cameras have distinct optical centres and overlap only marginally, and content that crosses boundary is split between two separately generated images. Cross-view consistency then has to be enforced by attention between views, by conditioning some views on others, or by concatenating the views into one canvas. Methods that lift generated video into 3D or 4D scenes [19, 65, 80] reconstruct from these per-camera videos and inherit their seams. We propose PanDWM, driving world model that generates the surround view as single 360 panorama  (Fig. 1)  . Instead of aligning six separately generated views, PanDWM places every camera boundary inside one image, 1 where cross-camera consistency becomes spatial continuity. The stitching map also gives each pixel source camera and its calibrated ray, which later anchor the 3D Gaussians. The network processes the panorama as two halves rather than six camera views, which also lowers the cost. Because camera images sample their periphery more densely, six views that are nowhere coarser than the panorama need 6240 tokens per frame against 4608, and the same network denoises and decodes the halves 1.17 faster (supplementary Sec. 2.5). Long videos are usually produced clip by clip [5, 33, 57], at tens of denoiser evaluations per clip and with gap between the recorded history seen in training and the generated history seen at inference [24]. PanDWM instead generates the panorama causally, one window at time, with four-step student trained on self-generated history. feed-forward decoder lifts each generated frame along the calibrated rays into 3D Gaussians for novel-view rendering. 4D Gaussians add ego-aligned static Gaussians from neighbouring frames, filling regions that the current frame does not observe along new trajectories. Our contributions are: Panoramic driving world modeling. We generate the surround view as one 360 panorama, which turns crosscamera consistency into spatial continuity at lower cost In the 360 view, PanDWM has lower than six views. FID and FVD than multi-camera baselines. four-step causal panoramic generator. blockcausal student trained on its own rollouts runs 846 faster than the baselines and matches the FID of its 50step teacher with 4 instead of 100 denoiser evaluations. Feed-forward 3D and 4D Gaussian lifting. decoder lifts generated latents along the source-camera rays into pixel-aligned Gaussians in one pass, and static Gaussians from neighbouring frames complete them into 4D scenes with the lowest depth error among camera-only methods. 2. Related work Driving video generation and world models. MagicDrive [14] introduced layout control for street-view images, conditioning on 3D boxes, road maps and text. Multi-camera video generators carry these conditions to six views [5, 15, 39, 48, 53, 55] and keep the views consistent through factorized cross-camera attention [53] or by placing the perspective images side by side on one canvas [76]. Others also predict semantics and metric depth [26] or bring occupancy and LiDAR into the generation [20, 25]. Longer videos come from conditioning on past frames [17, 21, 33, 57, 73], and recent models distil the generator to few denoising steps to lower the cost of such rollouts [9, 31, 72]. The panoramas of Panacea and OmniNWM are sets of surround cameras of this kind. In contrast, PanDWM generates the rig as one panorama in which every camera boundary lies inside the image. Panoramic generation. Panoramic video models build on perspective video diffusion. They adapt pretrained models to equirectangular distortion and the wrap-around seam [45, 56], outpaint perspective clips to the full sphere [32, 41], or generate perspective views jointly before stitching them [58]. DynamicScaler [30] slides its denoising window over canvases of arbitrary size, and PanoWorld [27] follows camera trajectories in aerial scenes. Each frame in these models has single projection centre, and no camera rig or driving layout is involved. In driving, panoramas have served BEV mapping [12, 52] and controllable street-view images [42], and QuaDreamer [54] generates panoramic video for quadruped robots. None of them generates panoramic driving video from scene layouts. Few-step autoregressive video diffusion. Autoregressive video diffusion assigns noise levels per token [4] or lets noise grow across temporal chunks for streaming [37]. Few-step causal generators are distilled from slower teacher, by distribution matching distillation (DMD) [67, 68] from bidirectional teacher in CausVid [69] or by consistency distillation [40] from an autoregressive teacher in Causal Forcing++ [77]. student trained only on recorded context drifts once it conditions on its own outputs. Self Forcing [24] therefore rolls the student out during training, CausalDrive [61] combines this with DMD for real-time front-view driving, and Self-Forcing++ [11] and LongLive [64] extend generation to minutes. Adversarial losses further sharpen few-step samples [29, 38, 67]. PanDWM brings self-rollout distillation with an adversarial loss on rollouts to layout-conditioned panoramic driving video. From video to 3D and 4D scenes. Per-scene optimization fits Gaussians to recorded driving videos [7, 62], to generated videos [16, 79], or to recordings augmented with generated views [35, 75]. FreeVS [46] instead synthesizes novel trajectories with conditional video diffusion and no explicit geometry. Feed-forward methods predict Gaussians in one pass from pixel-aligned features [3, 6, 60], surround-view inputs [43], pixelvoxel representations [51] or volumes [34]. Driving-specific models extend VGGT to 4D [70], enforce photometric and geometric consistency across views [49] or aggregate frames through Gaussian velocities [63]. Some generative world models output such scenes directly. WorldSplat [80] decodes multi-view latents into pixel-aligned Gaussians and accumulates static geometry, DiST-4D [19] generates metric depth with the video, and X-Scene [65] and Drive2Gauss [78] lift generated scenes into 3D or 4D Gaussians. Reconstructed panoramas [66, 71] are equirectangular images with one centre each. In contrast, our decoder lifts panoramic latents along the rays of the six source cameras. 2 Figure 2. PanDWM overview. (a) Panoramic history is split into overlapping halves and encoded by VAE. Conditioned on layouts, text and ray maps, causal diffusion transformer predicts 16 frames from 3 history frames in four steps; its final 3 frames seed the next window. (b) feed-forward decoder lifts frame latents into pixel-aligned Gaussians along calibrated source-camera rays, at ranges relabelled with Depth Anything 3. Static geometry from neighbouring frames supports 4D completion. Panoramas are displayed as cylindrical bands; ellipsoids are enlarged for display. 3. Method 3.2. Causal panoramic video diffusion PanDWM takes recorded panoramic history, 3D box and HD-map layouts and text prompt, and predicts future panoramic video that can be lifted into renderable Gaussian scenes  (Fig. 2)  . The panoramic band places every camera boundary inside one image (Sec. 3.1). blockcausal diffusion model generates the band window by window (Sec. 3.2), four-step student makes this generation fast and robust to its own history (Sec. 3.3), and feedforward decoder lifts each frame into 3D and 4D Gaussians (Sec. 3.4). 3.1. Panoramic band representation Six separately generated views have to agree at every camera boundary. We avoid such boundaries by generating one 360 33.3 panoramic band per frame. We stitch the six nuScenes images onto one azimuthelevation grid with the projection of OneBEV [52], which gives every pixel single source camera, and keep only the central 33.3 of elevation. The band is split into two overlapping halves of 2304256, which multi-view video backbone processes as two views per frame. Both cuts lie inside single cameras, the blended overlap in the front camera and the wrap-around in the rear one. Every camera boundary therefore lies within one half, and consistency across it becomes spatial continuity within single view. Backbone and conditioning. Each half is encoded by the Stable Diffusion 3.5 VAE. The denoiser is the diffusion transformer of Stable Diffusion 3 (SD3) [13] with UniMLVGs cross-view and temporal extensions [5], initialized from UniMLVG weights. To let the halves exchange information along the full 360 row at low cost, we use row-wise cross-half attention, in which each token row attends to the same row of both halves. Temporal attention runs over the window separately for each half. Class-coloured 3D box wireframes and HD-map outlines are stitched into the band like the images and enter through image-adapter residuals, while CLIP and T5 embeddings of short text prompt enter SD3s joint attention. Fourier-encoded rays of virtual pinhole camera facing each halfs centre condition the crossview and temporal blocks [5] and identify each half and its heading. Causality and teacher training. Autoregressive rollout requires that no frame sees the future. Each window contains 3 clean history frames and 16 target frames, and frameblock causal mask [64] lets each frame attend only to itself and earlier frames. The backbone has no temporal convolutions, and the mask alone determines causality. The history is excluded from the loss, and all target frames share one noise level in rectified-flow training [13]. The teacher samples with 50 guided Euler steps, and the last 3 output frames 3 of each window become the history of the next. 3.3. Four-step student trained on its own history Fifty guided steps cost 100 denoiser evaluations per window, and model trained on recorded history meets its own imperfect outputs as history at inference. We address both with four-step student trained on self-generated history. Initialization and sampling. The causal student fθ predicts clean latents and is initialized from the teacher by causal consistency distillation [40, 77]. It minimizes fθ(xσn ) sg[fθ(xσn+1)]2, where xσn+1 results from one guided teacher Euler step from σn to σn+1, θ is the moving average of θ and sg stops gradients. The student then generates each window in four unguided steps at σ {1, 0.9, 0.75, 0.5}, predicting clean latent and renoising it between steps. Training on self-generated history. Starting from 3 recorded frames, the student rolls out windows without gradients, and the final 3 generated frames become the history of the training window [24, 61]. Gradients flow through randomly selected denoising exit step of that window, and the history latents stay clean. DMD [67, 68] matches the students output distribution to the teachers. It uses the frozen guided teacher and fake-score network trained on student samples, both conditioned on the students history. Adversarial supervision. DMD pulls the student toward its teacher rather than toward recorded video. To anchor the student to recordings, we add spatial and temporal discriminators on intermediate fake-score features. Spatial heads score pooled tokens, and temporal heads score consecutiveframe differences. hinge loss compares generated windows with recordings at the same time steps and noise level, including the first window after recorded history. Motion and sharpness. We further match coarse motion, flicker and detail to the recorded latents. Let denote average pooling and Hx = UPx the high-frequency residual, with upsampling to the latent resolution. We compute three generated-to-recorded ratios: ρlf of the mean squared frame difference of Px, ρhf of the frame difference of Hx normalized by its energy, and ρe of the high-frequency energy. The losses are Lmm = [log ρhf]2 + + [log ρlf]2 Lsharp = [log 0.9 log ρe]2 +, + + [log 0.9 log ρlf]2 +, (1) (2) where []+ = max(, 0). The low-frequency term keeps coarse motion within 0.91 times the recordings, the highfrequency term penalizes flicker and the energy term discourages blur. Feed-forward Gaussian lifting Decoder and geometry. Adjacent pixels of the band can come from cameras with different optical centres. We therefore place each Gaussian on its own source-camera ray. We adapt the pixel-aligned Gaussian decoder of WorldSplat [80] to the band and train it from scratch. The decoder takes the panoramic latents and Plucker ray maps of the calibrated source-camera rays. Cross-half attention and convolutional upsampling then predict one Gaussian per pixel, with colour, opacity, scale, rotation, range dp and offset p. With c(p) the source camera of pixel p, the Gaussian centre is µp = oc(p) + dp rp + p, (3) where oc(p) is that cameras optical centre, rp the calibrated unit ray of p, dp [0.5, 400] range predicted in inverse depth, and learned offset across the ray, bounded to one decoder pixel. Unlike the virtual-camera rays that condition the video model, these rays keep the distinct sourcecamera origins. Both halves Gaussians are kept in the overlap  (Fig. 3)  . Supervision and depth relabelling. The Gaussians are rendered into the six nuScenes cameras, and the renders are differentiably stitched back into the band for panoramic L1, LPIPS and auxiliary depth losses [80]. Part of the 3D decoders training uses student-generated latents, with their VAE decodings as targets and no depth loss, so that the decoder also learns to lift predicted content. To improve the predicted ranges, each Gaussian is moved along its ray to the range that Depth Anything 3 [28] estimates from the input frames, jointly over the clip for 4D Gaussians. Pixels that Depth Anything 3 labels as sky or leaves without range keep dp. The decoder is fine-tuned with this relabelling so that its other attributes fit the new geometry. 4D Gaussians. single frame leaves regions unobserved along new trajectories. The conditioning 3D boxes separate dynamic from static Gaussians. The 4D decoder starts from the 3D one and is trained on multiple frames, whose static Gaussians are aligned by ego motion and combined with the target frames dynamic Gaussians. Leaveone-out reconstruction encourages complementary geometry, and an opacity coverage term encourages complete renders. At render time, aligned static Gaussians from neighbouring frames fill pixels that the current frame leaves uncovered, and the current frame keeps its dynamic content. For recorded input, only earlier frames are used. 4. Experiments 4.1. Setups Data. We train on the 700 training scenes of nuScenes [1] and evaluate on its 150 validation scenes. Annotated 3D boxes and HD maps are rendered into panoramic layout images as conditions (Sec. 3.1). Val-150 contains the first 3.5 of each validation scene, following the evaluation configuration of UniMLVG [5] in the OpenDWM repository [39], and serves as the benchmark for comparison with other methods. For longer horizons we use the 83 validation scenes that allow 19.5 rollout. Test-S takes three clips from each, starting 5, 10 and 15 in (249 clips), and TestL scores windows 312 of 19.5 rollout from each scene start. Both test sets are disjoint in time from Val-150. Ablations use the first 3.5 of 78 validation scenes (Dev-78), and checkpoints were selected on Dev-78 and on long rollouts of 12 of the 83 scenes. Val-150, Test-S and Dev-78 clips have 3 recorded history frames followed by 32 generated Figure 4. Band FVD-1 against time per frame on Val-150 (FID in Tab. 1); lower left is better. frames. Metrics. Video quality is measured with FID [22] and I3Dbased [2] FVD [44], where FVD-1 and FVD-2 cover the first and second 16-frame windows. The flicker ratio compares frame-to-frame changes of generated and recorded video on static scenes, with 1 as the reference, and the sharpness ratio compares their detail. Controllability is measured by object recall from Faster R-CNN [36] and road IoU from Mask2Former [8], and efficiency by denoiser evaluations (NFE) and time per frame. All methods are compared with equal sample counts and identical valid regions, alongside real-vs-real reference distances [10] and temporal measures [18]. For our method we report means and standard deviations over three seeds, with 95% scenelevel jackknife intervals. Evaluation spaces and baselines. We run UniMLVG [5], the SD3.5-based OpenDWM model [39], DreamForge [33], DiST-4D [19] and OmniNWM [26] with official weights and sampling settings (reproduction checks in supplementary Sec. 3). All of them predict from recorded history and are scored on the same 32 target frames of each Val150 clip, with 12 Hz outputs matched to these frames by LiDAR timestamp. DiST-4D and OmniNWM take single recorded frame as history, and OmniNWM receives no boxes or map. Quality is evaluated in the 4114 256 panoramic band that our model generates, into which baseline outputs are stitched with the OneBEV [52] mapping. For second evaluation, our band is mapped back into the six real camera views at 256 448. Gaussian baselines are DrivingForward [43], Omni-Scene [51], ReconDrive [70] and MCSplat [49]. Implementation details. We train in four stages on 8 GPUs with AdamW, with learning rates of 2106 for the student, 4 107 for the fake score and 3 105 for the discriminator heads, and an EMA decay of 0.99; the stages and other settings are in supplementary Sec. 1.4. 5 Table 1. Time is measured on one A40 including VAE decoding, per 0.1 of video (one frame at 10 Hz; DreamForge, DiST-4D and OmniNWM output 12 Hz). PanDWM is averaged over three seeds and baselines use seed 42. Comparison with driving video models Short-term prediction. PanDWM has lower FID, FVD-1 and FVD-2 in the band than every baseline and generates 8 to 46 times faster, at 1.96 per frame (Tab. 1 and Fig. 4). It also has higher object recall and road IoU than DreamForge, DiST-4D and OmniNWM. Generating the band natively avoids the resampling loss of six-view outputs. Recorded views at 256 448 already score 17.9 FID once stitched into the band, whereas mapping the band into the six cameras costs 0.63 FID on recorded data. In the six cameras, PanDWM also has the lowest FID (5.34). At camera boundaries it adds no seams beyond those of recorded video, unlike four of the five baselines (supplementary Sec. 5). Confidence intervals and the full six-camera evaluation are in supplementary Sec. 2.1. Front-view world models. We also compare the front view of our panoramas with HorizonDrive [72], Epona [73], Vista [17] and GEM [21] on 149 of the Val-150 clips (Fig. 5; settings in supplementary Sec. 3). The data loader used for these runs excludes scene-0018, in which one frame is 50.5 ms off, beyond its 50 ms synchronization tolerance (Val-150 uses 51 ms). At 2.5 s, PanDWM keeps the marked objects in place, whereas the front-view models lose or displace them. Multi-camera comparison. The refiner is copy of our causal teacher, conditioned on the rendered latents through zeroinitialized branch and trained to restore recorded frames It trades some cross-shift consistency for from renders. per-view fidelity (supplementary Sec. 1.7). Conclusion We presented PanDWM, driving world model that generates the surround view as single 360 panoramic band. four-step block-causal student, trained on self-generated history, generates the band window by window, and feedforward decoder lifts the generated latents along calibrated source-camera rays into 3D Gaussians, which static Gaussians from neighbouring frames complete into 4D scenes. Limitations and Future Work. (1) Each window sees only the last three generated frames, and Test-L FVD grows from 86.6 (windows 35) to 126.6 (windows 911). Renders of the accumulated static Gaussians could serve as longer memory. (2) 4D completion covers only static content, leaving unseen parts of moving objects empty; aligning them with the 3D boxes is left for future work.

sections.title: Supplementary Material
sections.content: 1. Implementation details 1.1. Panoramic preprocessing and conditions Drawing on OneBEV [52], the six nuScenes images are mapped to 9600 900 canvas spanning 360 in azimuth and 25 in elevation. Keeping rows [150, 750) gives 9600 600 band with 33.3 vertical coverage. The halves use columns [0, 5376) and [4224, 9600), each spanning 201.6. Their 1152-column overlap (43.2) lies inside the front-camera region. Each half is resized to 2304 256. For display and evaluation, removing the right halfs 494 overlapping columns gives 4114 256 band, with 128column raised-cosine cross-fade replacing the hard cut. The rear seam wraps from column 9600 to column 0 within the rear-camera region, without overlap or blending. The two layout inputs are class-coloured 3D box wireframes and HD map outlines. Map elements comprise drivable areas, lanes, pedestrian crossings, walkways, stop lines and car parks within 65 m. The condition panoramas come from the same release as the RGB panoramas; our renderer for these conditions draws each camera with its calibration and stitches the results with the RGB mapping, so that corresponding condition and RGB pixels share source camera. 1.2. Video architecture and causal teacher The SD3.5 VAE produces 32288 latent with 16 channels for each half. patch size of 2 gives 16 144 = 2304 tokens. The denoiser uses the 24-layer SD3 transformer [13], extended and initialized from UniMLVG [5]. Cross-view and temporal self-attention blocks follow layers 1, 5, 9, 13, 17 and 21, with learned scalar gates blending their outputs into the main stream. Row-wise cross-view attention exchanges same-row tokens between both halves, while temporal attention operates over all window tokens of each half. Concatenated box and map images enter an image adapter whose residuals are added to the first six transformer blocks. CLIP and T5 encode text for SD3s joint attention. Each its halfs virtual pinhole camera faces the halfs centre; Fourier-encoded ray map is added to the cross-view and temporal block inputs. These conditioning rays differ from the calibrated source-camera rays used for Gaussian placement. Windows contain 19 frames at 10 Hz, with 3 clean history frames excluded from the loss and 16 targets sharing noise level σ. Seams at camera boundaries To measure seams, we average the absolute horizontal luminance difference between neighbouring columns of the stitched band over rows, the 32 scored frames and the 150 Val-150 clips. At column b, the seam ratio sums this profile over columns 2 to + 2, subtracts four times its mean over the columns 4 to 10 away from on both sides, and divides by that mean; it is close to 1 without seam and to the step size for one-column step. Recorded panoramas already have seams at the six camera boundaries, from exposure and parallax differences (ratio 10.28), and stitching 256 448 camera views adds more (14.95). We therefore report each methods excess over recorded views at its own resolution, stitched in the same way, with 95% intervals from 2000 scene-bootstrap resamples. Table S6 shows that PanDWM adds no seam at the cam9 era boundaries, like UniMLVG and the teacher, whereas OpenDWM, DiST-4D, DreamForge and OmniNWM add 1.3 to 2.4 over their references. Most of the difference in raw ratios therefore comes from stitching low-resolution camera views rather than from inconsistency between generated views. Behind the vehicle, where the two halves meet without overlap, PanDWM adds seam of +2.15; the teacher shows the same seam (+1.99), so it comes from the two-half representation rather than from distillation. At the front joint, the 128-column cross-fade removes the seam (+0.01, [0.04, 0.06], against +0.62, [0.56, 0.69] for hard cut). The ratio is local and does not detect content mismatches that keep local gradients unchanged. Varying the cross-fade width (0, 32, 64, 128, 256 or 494 of the 494 overlapping columns) changes only the front joint; the rear joint and the camera boundaries are unchanged. Relative to the 128 columns we use, hard cut adds front seam of +0.62 and raises FVD-1 by 0.25 ([0.11, 0.39]), and 64 columns still raise FVD-1 by 0.08 ([0.004, 0.15]). Wider blends lower FID slightly (0.08 at 494 columns) by blurring the blend zone, whose gradient energy drops by 6.6%; FVD-2 does not change with the width. 10 6.
